extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, agency lawyers, judges, and advanced law students
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative framework for assessing procedural defects in agency rulemaking (notice-and-comment, good-cause exceptions, logical-outgrowth), and for deciding appropriate remedies (vacatur, harmless-error). Focuses on factors courts consider and circuit splits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical-outgrowth (final rule must be a logical outgrowth of proposal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Final rules must be a 'logical outgrowth' of the proposed rule so that the public has 'reasonably specific notice' that the changes adopted were among the range of alternatives being considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts examine whether the proposed rule put the public on notice of the particular change (e.g., bright-line distance limits). Even when agencies discussed categories of alternatives (e.g., 'distance limitations'), failure to specify particular limits can lead courts to find lack of notice. Examples: Sixth Circuit found bright-line distance limits not a logical outgrowth where the proposal used a standard rather than fixed distances; Allina (D.C. Cir.) found agency pulled a 'surprise switcheroo' despite binary issue being 'in play'. Consider whether regulated parties or other commentators actually addressed the specific change during the comment period and whether other venues furnished notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prejudice requirement in notice-and-comment challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether and how a challenger must show prejudice from the procedural defect; courts 'have not required a particularly robust showing of prejudice in notice-and-comment cases.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some courts demand little showing of prejudice; others demand demonstration that the lack of notice prevented focused opposition. Even detailed comments in the record may be dismissed as insufficiently 'focused' by some courts (Allina). Assess both the existence of actual comment on the issue and the court's willingness to treat that as prejudicial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity of notice is required (more than generic alternatives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should provide sufficiently specific notice of the alternatives they are considering; generic references to possibilities (e.g., 'distance limitations') may be inadequate to satisfy §553 notice requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the agency failed to spell out the particular limits it had in mind, a court may conclude the public lacked 'reasonably specific notice' (In re EPA). But evidence that the topic was repeatedly raised in comments and meetings may mitigate that failure. Weigh whether the record shows the public could meaningfully comment on the particular choices later adopted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent and diversity of public engagement as evidence of notice
rubrics_metrics.description: The breadth of outreach (reports, advisory boards, hundreds of meetings, multiple public hearings, millions of comments) can indicate that the agency 'courted public input' and that the public had opportunities to comment on core issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies that convene scientific advisory boards, publish review reports, hold many stakeholder meetings, and receive large comment volumes can argue that the procedural defect caused little real prejudice. Courts vary in how much weight they give such engagement; some courts still vacate despite extensive engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmless error doctrine in administrative context
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a procedural violation can be excused under a harmless-error analysis; courts are split and generally skeptical of applying harmless error to notice-and-comment violations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some circuits refuse to accept post hoc harmlessness (Fifth Circuit warning about making §553 unenforceable); D.C. Circuit is slightly more flexible but requires a 'compelling showing' that the agency kept an open mind. Scholars (Hickman & Thomson) argue for a strong presumption that postpublication comment does not cure defects. Consider circuit precedent, severity of procedural lapse, and whether the agency actually considered the same substantive issues in the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postpublication (postpromulgation) comment as potential cure
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether soliciting comments after publishing a rule can cure an initial notice-and-comment defect depends on whether the agency remained 'open minded' and made a 'compelling showing' that later notice was adequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts differ: the Fifth Circuit rejects such cures in most cases; the D.C. Circuit accepts them only with compelling evidence that the agency kept an open mind; other circuits vacate despite postpublication comments (e.g., SORNA cases). Examine whether the agency formally invited comments, responded to them, republished a proposal, and whether the final rule materially changed after comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-cause exception must be narrowly construed
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies may avoid notice-and-comment when 'good cause' exists (impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to public interest), but courts review such determinations closely and usually construe the exception narrowly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: D.C. Circuit says it owes 'no particular deference' on good-cause determinations (Mack Trucks). Vacatur is the conventional remedy when courts disagree with an agency's good-cause finding. Consider whether the agency's urgency rationale is reasonable (public safety, imminent harm) and whether Congress intended waiver of APA procedures in the statutory delegation context (e.g., SORNA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedial purity: courts' predisposition to vacate
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts often exhibit a commitment to 'remedial purity,' leading them to vacate rules for procedural lapses even when the substantive impact appears minimal or parties had ample opportunity to influence outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This predisposition explains many vacaturs despite extensive record participation or lack of demonstrated prejudice. When assessing likely remedy, consider the court's tone in precedent and whether it emphasizes strict enforcement of procedural norms over practical harms or benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of regulated parties' prior involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether parties challenging the rule had participated extensively in the rulemaking (comments, meetings, hearings, advisory committees) affects whether the court views the procedural error as prejudicial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heavy prior involvement (long-standing engagement, named participants at hearings, prior comments) undercuts claims of surprise and prejudice; however, some courts have still vacated rules despite such involvement (International Union v. MSHA, Allina). Document the challenger’s documented participation and whether specific objections were aired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy of agency response to comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts assess whether an agency gave a 'palpably adequate' response to significant comments; inadequate responses can justify vacatur even if notice procedures were followed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'palpably inadequate' response (or failure to respond) is a separate procedural deficiency. Agencies that respond at length to comments and explain their reasoning fare better. Example: CAB’s inadequate response led to vacatur; subsequent reissuance without fresh notice was also problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material alteration vs. technical correction
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a change is a mere technical correction or a material amendment affecting regulated parties' obligations determines whether notice-and-comment is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an amendment 'materially altered the obligations' of regulated parties (Utility Solid Waste Activities Group), vacatur is likely even if the agency characterized the change as correcting a mistake. Consider whether the change expands substantive obligations, coverage, or compliance costs compared to the original proposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular caution when criminal consequences are involved
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts are especially reluctant to apply harmless-error reasoning when a procedurally defective rule has criminal consequences (e.g., SORNA retroactivity affecting prosecutions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When rulemaking affects criminal liability, several circuits have invalidated interim rules issued without notice and comment despite post-issuance procedures. Evaluate the severity of rights at stake and the likelihood courts will demand strict procedural compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency openness / 'kept an open mind' requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: For curative postpromulgation procedures to succeed, agencies must show they kept an open mind and genuinely considered post-issuance comments rather than foreclosing debate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts look for evidence the agency considered comments anew and altered its position when appropriate (Air Transp. Ass'n; McClouth Steel). If the record indicates the agency had effectively decided in advance, later comment periods are unlikely to cure defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of alternative venues and prior comment channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether issues were raised in other channels (meetings, advisory board reports, stakeholder consultations) counts as part of the notice-and-comment context and may mitigate defects in the formal NPRM.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts vary on the weight given to non-NPRM engagement; extensive pre-proposal engagement (science reviews, advisory board letters, hundreds of meetings) strengthens the agency's position that stakeholders had notice, but some courts remain unwilling to treat such engagement as substituting for required procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts’ circuit-by-circuit variance (precedent matters)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is significant circuit split on deference for good-cause findings, the curative power of postpublication comment, and the standard for harmless error in rulemaking contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess applicable circuit precedent: some circuits (Fifth, Third, Ninth, Eighth) have rejected cures or found no good cause in key contexts; others (Fourth, Eleventh) have accepted agency urgency in SORNA; D.C. Circuit has its own tests (narrow construction, 'no particular deference', 'compelling showing'). Consult controlling circuit law when predicting outcomes.
